shape memory materials: shape memory alloys (SMAs)
shape memory materials: shape memory polymers (SMPs)
stimuli-responsive polymers and gels (thermal, magnetic, optical/light, humidity, pH, chemical, and bio-hydrogel swelling)
constitutive_assumptions: Continuous deformation of hyperelastic materials in soft structures without rigid joints
Viscoelastic behavior in electrorheological and magnetorheological suspensions under electric or magnetic fields
Electrostatic Maxwell stress causing elastomer membrane thinning and planar expansion in dielectric elastomer actuators
Crystallographic phase transitions between martensite and austenite phases in shape memory alloys
Phase transitions involving crystallization-melting or vitrification-glass transitions in shape memory polymers

Substrate surface condition (dry, clean, smooth, rough, porous, or nonporous)
Preloading normal contact force in geckoadhesion
Initial geometric configuration and structural boundary constraints of gripper fingers or bags
dependent_variables: Lifting ratio (object mass to gripper mass)
Bending stroke, angle, or expansion strain
Response time and phase transition rate
Adhesion pressure in normal and shear directions
Stiffness variation range / relative stiffness change
Graspable object size range and allowable object geometry

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Soft gripping technologies can be systematically categorized into three main operating mechanisms: actuation, controlled stiffness, and controlled adhesion, which can also be combined into hybrid systems.
Material compliance and underactuation allow soft grippers to passively conform to varied object geometries, lowering control complexity via morphological computation.

Fluidic elastomer actuators (FEAs) generate high blocked forces (e.g., 80 N at 300 kPa and 112 N at 200 kPa) and large bending angles, but are constrained by the mass and size of external compressors and fluidic channel impedance restricting response frequencies above 1 Hz.

Dielectric elastomer actuators (DEAs) offer rapid response times under 200 microseconds and high strains, but produce low active stress and generally require high operating voltages on the order of kilovolts.

Granular jamming enables rapid reversible stiffness changes up to 24 times via vacuum-induced depressurization of granule-filled membranes, producing caging forces without high normal compressive loads, but cannot envelop flat objects.

Low-melting point alloys (LMPAs) embedded in soft matrices demonstrate relative stiffness changes ranging from 25 to over 9000 times through thermal phase changes between 47 °C and 62 °C, though cooling times typically exceed 60 seconds.

Electrorheological (ER) and magnetorheological (MR) fluids transition to viscoelastic states within 10 milliseconds upon application of electric or magnetic fields, but their overall solidified stiffness is constrained by yield stresses up to 250 kPa.

Controlled adhesion mechanisms such as electroadhesion and geckoadhesion produce high shear holding forces with minimal normal compressive forces, enabling high lifting ratios (reported up to 286.7 for geckoadhesion and 54.7 for electroadhesion), but require clean and dry surfaces.

Integrating stretchable resistive, capacitive, optical waveguide, and magnetic Hall-effect sensors into compliant gripper structures facilitates proprioceptive finger curvature detection and exteroceptive object tactile characterization.

experimental_setup: Compiled literature experimental setups evaluating blocked forces and load-lifting ratios using dead weights, force gauges, and pulling fixtures
Substrate adhesion testing setups measuring normal and shear detachment pressures on diverse test surfaces (glass, paper, metal)
Deep-sea robotic sampling apparatus mounted on remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) operating at 1200 m water depth
Empirical prehension trials grasping fragile, deformable, flat, and living targets (eggs, fruits, live mice, goldfish, glassware, sheet materials)
future_work: Developing miniaturized, integrated soft fluidic pumps and transducers (such as electrohydrodynamic units) to enhance portability of fluidic elastomer grippers
Accelerating thermal cooling and phase transition rates in LMPAs and SMPs via thermally conductive elastomer matrices, circulating fluid channels, or electrocaloric units
Reducing actuation hysteresis in SMAs through magnetization and in SMPs via tailored polymer blending
Integrating controlled adhesion or variable stiffness mechanisms into DEAs and jamming grippers to grasp flat and highly deformable objects
Improving geckoadhesive performance on rough surfaces using microspines and enhanced pillar geometries, as well as incorporating self-cleaning properties
Exploring self-healing polymers, recyclable formulations, and biodegradable or edible materials for sustainable and transient robotic devices
Embedding stretchable multimodal distributed sensor networks (strain, pressure, optical, temperature, biochemical) paired with local signal processing for autonomous prehension
Extending soft prehension mechanisms into whole-body robot prehension, locomotion, and shape control
independent_variables: Fluidic actuation pressure and vacuum level in FEAs and granular jamming systems
Electric voltage and electric field intensity in DEAs, IPMCs, electroadhesion, and ER fluids
Heating current and temperature in SMAs, SMPs, and LMPAs
Magnetic field intensity in MR fluids and magnetic polymer grippers
Chemical stimulus level (pH, ion/salt concentration, solvent presence, humidity)
Geometric dimensions (aspect ratios, chamber walls, electrode spacing, fiber reinforcement patterns)
limitations_inferred: Performance metrics compiled across heterogeneous published studies reflect differing experimental methodologies and setups rather than standardized benchmarking protocols

Long-term durability and environmental resilience of novel stimuli-responsive polymers (e.g., UV, dust, moisture, and temperature fluctuations) remain largely unaddressed under real-world industrial settings
Combining multiple functional modalities (e.g., actuation plus variable stiffness and sensing) substantially increases manufacturing complexity and failure modes
limitations_stated_by_authors: Miniaturization of fluidic elastomer and externally motorized grippers is constrained by heavy and bulky external pumps, compressors, and motor assemblies
FEA actuation frequencies above 1 Hz are difficult to achieve due to fluidic channel impedance and required flow rates
DEAs produce low active output stress, necessitating multilayer stacking that complicates device fabrication
High operational voltages (several kilovolts) in DEAs and electroadhesion introduce risk of external electrical discharges
IPMC actuators exhibit slow operating response, low output stress, poor thermodynamic efficiency, and actuation hysteresis
Thermal variable-stiffness materials (LMPAs, SMPs, SMAs) suffer from slow solidifying and cooling response times dominated by thermal conduction and convective dissipation
SMAs exhibit cyclic actuation hysteresis, require high electric driving currents, and possess low thermodynamic efficiency
Granular jamming grippers cannot grasp flat objects due to inability to envelope/cage them, and cannot adjust to shape changes of deformable objects once solidified
ER and MR fluids provide relatively low absolute structural stiffness due to limited yield stress (up to 250 kPa)
Electroadhesion and geckoadhesion require clean and relatively dry target surfaces, and electroadhesion exhibits residual charge hysteresis upon voltage removal
Geckoadhesion struggles to adhere to rough surfaces and low surface-energy materials, and highly compliant substrates may hinder target release
Suction mechanisms require smooth, nonporous object surfaces to maintain vacuum seals
Elastomeric components often suffer from a lack of long-term mechanical robustness
Resistive strain sensors display history-dependent resistance (hysteresis) that complicates calibration, whereas capacitive sensors require more complex readout circuitry
main_results: Formulated a taxonomy dividing soft prehension into three core technology pillars: gripping by actuation, controlled stiffness, and controlled adhesion

Demonstrated that geckoadhesion achieves the highest published object-to-gripper lifting ratios (up to 286.7), with SMP systems reaching ratios up to 925, whereas FEAs reach lifting ratios up to 68 with high blocked forces
Confirmed that controlled stiffness mechanisms allow compliant enveloping of delicate objects followed by rigid caging, minimizing normal compressive contact stresses

Showed that controlled adhesion technologies (electroadhesion, geckoadhesion) generate high shear holding forces without requiring high normal pinch forces, enabling grasping of flat and delicate objects

Demonstrated that hybrid gripping configurations combining multiple physical principles (e.g., DEAs with electroadhesion, or FEAs with LMPAs or granular jamming) overcome individual technology limitations
Reviewed integration of flexible and stretchable sensor modalities to achieve closed-loop feedback, proprioceptive shape estimation, and tactile object recognition
modeling_methods: Topological optimization for the design of compliant mechanism grasping structures
Morphological computation concepts evaluating control complexity reduction achieved through structural compliance
Scaling laws governing physical actuation and surface-force dominance below 50 micrometers
performance_metrics: Adhesion pressure in normal and shear directions [kPa]
possible_gap_implications: Developing lightweight, integrated soft transducers for fluid pressurization and rapid cooling architectures would allow autonomous, untethered mobile soft robotic manipulation outside laboratory settings
Establishing standardized benchmarking protocols across diverse soft gripper technologies would enable objective cross-comparison and accelerate industrial adoption
paper.research_objective: To provide a comprehensive and critical review of soft robotic grippers across different material sets, physical operating principles, and device architectures, categorizing technologies into gripping by actuation, controlled stiffness, and controlled adhesion.
paper.research_problem: High mechanical and control complexity in conventional rigid robotic grippers, making it difficult to achieve human-like flexibility and dexterity and safely manipulate delicate, fragile, or deformable objects without damage.
paper.title: Soft Robotic Grippers
